title: Self-Regulation and the Jurisdiction Gap
hook: When a private body governs an activity but sits outside every regulator's remit, weak rules stop being a flaw and start being a competitive advantage.
key_points: Much of public life is governed by private associations whose authority comes from membership rules, not statute.
Oversight regimes are usually written for named bodies, so an organization outside the definition simply isn't covered.
If compliance costs money and non-compliance doesn't, the least-regulated body can undercut the rest on price and hassle.
ProPublica reports the AAU — a youth sports nonprofit serving 760,000 athletes and coaches — falls outside SafeSport's jurisdiction.
Its abuse cases were judged by an elected five-member board with no training in law, investigation, or child protection.
Mandatory arbitration in registration forms kept disputes out of open court, a rarity among comparable youth sports organizations.
content_html: A surprising amount of public life is governed not by government but by private associations: leagues, professional bodies, accreditation councils, standards groups. Their authority comes from membership rules rather than statute, and that usually works well enough — until you ask who watches them. Oversight regimes tend to be written for a named list of organizations, so a body that falls outside the definition is not lightly regulated; it is simply not covered. ProPublica's Molly Hensley-Clancy reports on one such case: the Amateur Athletic Union, a nonprofit serving 760,000 youth athletes and coaches, sits outside the jurisdiction of SafeSport, the center that handles abuse cases for U.S. Olympic-affiliated governing bodies.
extra_html:
The reporting describes what fills that vacuum. Abuse allegations went to a Board of Review of five elected regional members with no training in law, investigation, or child protection; a former board member of 25 years told ProPublica that decisions came down to "we just decided on our feelings." Registration forms required confidential arbitration, keeping disputes out of open court in a way ProPublica calls extremely rare among comparable youth sports organizations. The AAU is not required to honor SafeSport's public list of more than 2,500 banned or suspended coaches, and reporters identified eight coaches who worked with AAU teams within five years despite bans or suspensions elsewhere. After the journalists sent questions, the organization changed its website's description of abuse-prevention training from "mandatory" to "encouraged."

The structural lesson generalizes past sports. When a private body is uncovered, the missing rules are not just a safety problem — they are a price advantage, because compliance costs money and skipping it is legal. That is what makes gaps in coverage self-reinforcing rather than self-correcting, and why the durable fixes are boring ones: define oversight by the activity rather than by a list of member organizations, make ban lists portable across bodies, and limit confidential arbitration where the alleged harm is to a child.

related.hook: Governments can delegate the job of locking someone up. What often fails to travel with the contract is the duty to open the records.

related.title: Accountability & Oversight
related.hook: Power left unwatched drifts toward abuse. Accountability is the demand that officials answer for what they do — and oversight is the machinery that makes them.

related.title: Regulatory Capture
related.hook: Who protects a city's drinking water when the industry that put it at risk is also the one the regulator was built to serve? That's the problem political scientists call regulatory capture.

related.title: Interest Groups & Lobbying
related.hook: Between elections, organized groups press their case to government every day. Lobbying is how that pressure is applied — and it's both a feature and a worry of democracy.

prereqs.title: Accountability & Oversight
prereqs.hook: Power left unwatched drifts toward abuse. Accountability is the demand that officials answer for what they do — and oversight is the machinery that makes them.

flashcards.prompt: What is a jurisdiction gap in an oversight regime?
flashcards.back_html: An activity is governed by a private body, but the body falls outside the definition of who the oversight regime covers — so no regulator is responsible for it, even though the same risks are present.

flashcards.prompt: Why can a gap in oversight coverage make weak safeguards spread rather than shrink?

choices.text: Uncovered bodies carry lower compliance costs, so they can undercut regulated ones on fees and hassle
Regulators are legally required to lower standards to match the weakest body
Members generally prefer organizations with stricter rules, so coverage makes no difference

flashcards.explanation_html: Compliance is a cost. If skipping it is legal and cheaper, the uncovered organization competes on being easier to join — the gap becomes a selling point rather than an embarrassment.

flashcards.prompt: Why does mandatory arbitration in a membership form weaken public accountability?

choices.text: Disputes are resolved confidentially, so facts that a public trial would expose never reach the record
It removes the organization's legal liability entirely under federal law
It requires a government agency to take over the investigation

flashcards.explanation_html: Open courts generate a public record; confidential arbitration does not. Patterns that would surface across many lawsuits stay invisible.

flashcards.prompt: Why is an internal complaint board a weak substitute for external oversight?
flashcards.back_html: It is chosen by, and answerable to, the organization it judges — and, as ProPublica found at the AAU, its members may have no training in law, investigation, or child protection.
